beta_new: Start to the left of the approach boulder, follow the ramp as it climbs rightward through the gap between the cliff and a boulder, then keep traversing rightward beyond a piton for roughly thirty feet.
Sustained crack climbing that stays clean and steep.

moves.from: taking gear up to about 3 inches

beta_new: Go easily up to the roof, then pull directly over its lip. On the slab above, a couple more bolts lead to a lowering anchor, or you can continue another fifteen feet up pocketed rock to the summit.
Begin behind a pine, work up flakes, and clip three bolts set close together to reach a ledge. Then shift right and complete the climb via the neighboring Straight Flush line.
Begin in the little crack that bends rightward (the first bolt is right below it) and follow six bolts upward along the north side. Past the final bolt, bear leftward onto the shoulder.
Begin in a scoop and angle rightward, clipping a trio of bolts, to reach a cave holding a fixed pin. Step left there and keep climbing, clipping another bolt or two.
Pitch one is closely bolted, with four bolts in about fifty feet. Pitch two relies mostly on cams to 3 inches and ends with three bolts below the anchors.
Four bolts lead up onto a slanting ledge, and a fifth bolt sits on the rounded arete higher up. The route can now be finished straight up.
Clip two bolts to reach the hard section of the neighboring route and join it there; the second pitch crosses the upper face with a single bolt.
A roof problem roughly twenty feet off the deck; the landing is friendlier than typical, and two bolts were added for those who want security.

To skip the opening difficulties, a ledge of easy scrambling gives a shorter, gentler first pitch. Taking the summit block directly at the finish is protectable with small cams slotted into the horizontal crack beneath it.
Starting from the ground, work the cracks in the dark stone hidden behind a spiny bush up to a ledge, then take a grittier crack above onto a pinnacle top fitted with two bolts.
Begin to the left of a low roof and climb easy ramps toward the right. Where they run out, clip two bolts; broken ground then leads to the higher diagonal crack belonging to Fault Line.
Start off boulders and clip a bolt en route to a minor ledge. Four variations leave from there, differing in how they handle the ceiling above.
A cut-off tree trunk partway up the crack makes the route easy to identify. The crack is wide enough in places to swallow a climber.

moves.from: so bring gear up to about 3.5 inches

beta_new: Ascend the corner, going by a fixed piton; once it ends, step upward and rightward, clipping a bolt, and carry on to the summit.
Climb a chimney, step out to the wall, and clip a bolt as you enter a rightward-slanting crack, which merges with Bisk around the midpoint of that route's opening pitch.

Step off a boulder, climb the wall beside a bolt, step across the crack arriving from your left, then go on up the higher wall with one further bolt, merging with Searching For Strippers close to its finish.
The first pitch passes four bolts, and the second pitch consists of a brief crack finishing at a ledge.

Clip the second bolt of the neighboring route, downclimb, then start this line to the right and angle across past a pre-clipped bolt. One awkward move takes cams, and you then continue to the neighbor's final bolt.
An eye-catching finger crack with a single bolt about one-third of the height up.
Begin in the crack that cuts the south face and climb it, then angle leftward beyond a bolt before returning rightward for the final stretch.
Climb the fingercrack until you can bridge across to the chockstone's left flank, then downclimb off it.

Pass a shrub and a bolt on the wall to gain a corner, then sidestep right over the wall beyond another bolt to the chimney's foot. Inside the chimney two fixed pitons appear, after which the going eases toward the summit.
Starting from the lower bolts works fine, while the original toprope version entered by moving across a horizontal crack from the right.
Climb up, then go left in the horizontal to reach a thin crack and follow it to the top. A bolt on a neighboring route can now be used for protection.
Step off a boulder and head up a four-bolt line; the route veers sharply leftward in the stretch after bolt three.

Begin like the two routes before it, then angle rightward to a bolt sitting above a horizontal break. Veer leftward until Overpass's slanting crack finishes, then climb vertically past one more bolt to join Overhang Bypass where its opening pitch ends.

Launch from a boulder tucked behind a tree and go rightward along a dike, clipping a bolt, then straight upward through four further bolts and leftward to a bolted belay. One more bolt, missing its hanger, remains above.
Ascend a groove that turns into a fist crack, beside the bolted chute on its right.
Three bolts protect a narrow face covered in buckets, and the highest of them is placed well up.
Begin at the wall's left edge and angle rightward across the patina plates toward a pair of bolts near the summit.

Begin beside a conspicuous tree with three trunks, climb leftward to a piton hammered into the arch, then rightward to a bolt. Work upward and leftward, then swing back toward the right to get over the headwall; easier ground leads to a belay with two bolts.
A crack leads onto a gritty face, which has one bolt.
Go up the gully, move right into a crack, and finish past two bolts.
On its own separate face, climb to a little pocket and then continue up the wall above, clipping a bolt.

Expect thin fingers on pitch two, where the hardest moves surmount a bulge. Higher up you stem a shallow dihedral and swing out through a roof, then merge with the neighbouring route for the finish.

Pitch one starts mid-ledge, jams up to a slender corner, and gets over a roof with a single 5.9 pull.

moves.from: A regular trad rack of nuts and cams is enough.

value.text: A regular trad rack of nuts and cams.

beta_new:
This is a long, wandering line that weaves across two neighbouring routes and keeps drifting left, so staying on route matters more than any single hard move.

Difficulties are scattered: the runout outer face of a tall corner midway, then a short downclimb of a slim arcing seam to reach a ramp, and finally delicate climbing near the top.
Head up to the little overhang, shuffle rightward onto the low-angle arete, and follow it to the ledge. Bolts here were removed and gear is scarce, so it is best treated as a toprope problem.

A big ramp is scrambled for a few hundred feet before real climbing starts. The hardest section is a nasty wide crack on pitch 10, and pitch 11 follows with frightening face moves protected by an old bolt.

Carry a generous rack: RPs, nuts, doubles of cams to #4 (three #4s), plus wide-crack protection like big tri-cams or tube chocks. A thin piton may help on pitch 12.
